topics.name: Battle of Chancellorsville
topics.kicker: Lee’s great 1863 victory over Hooker · Stonewall Jackson shot by his own men
topics.briefing: In May 1863, Robert E. Lee faced a Union army more than twice the size of his own near a crossroads in the Virginia woods called Chancellorsville. Lee boldly split his army and sent Stonewall Jackson on a secret march around the Union flank, and the surprise attack sent Joseph Hooker’s army reeling. But that night, Jackson was accidentally shot by his own men, and he died eight days later.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Chancellorsville (do not accept “Battle of the Wilderness” or “Fredericksburg”)

tossups.p: On the night of May 2, 1863, during this battle, soldiers of the 18th North Carolina Infantry fired into a group of riders returning from a scouting trip in the dark, mistaking them for Union cavalry.
tossups.r: That volley badly wounded their own general, Stonewall Jackson. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia, a victory for Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: Ernest Hemingway took the title of his 1950 novel _Across the River and into the Trees_ from the last words of a general who was wounded in this battle. That general said, “Let us cross over the river and rest under the shade of the trees.”
tossups.r: That general, Stonewall Jackson, died of pneumonia eight days after he was shot by his own men. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle won by Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: On the night of May 1, 1863, two generals sat on empty cracker boxes and planned a daring march after cavalry under Fitzhugh Lee found that the Union right flank was “in the air,” protected by no river or hill.
tossups.r: The next day, Stonewall Jackson’s men marched around that flank and attacked. For 10 points, name this battle in which Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: During this battle, a cannonball struck a porch pillar that a Union commander was leaning against at a brick house, leaving him dazed. Earlier that morning, May 3, he had ordered his troops to give up Hazel Grove, a clearing where Confederate cannons soon set up.
tossups.r: That commander was Joseph Hooker. For 10 points, name this battle in Virginia, Robert E. Lee’s greatest victory.

tossups.p: While the main armies fought to the west during this battle, John Sedgwick’s Union corps captured Marye’s Heights at Fredericksburg, but it was stopped at Salem Church and had to retreat across the Rappahannock River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Stonewall Jackson was accidentally shot by his own troops, a loss Lee compared to losing his own right arm.

tossups.p: Before this battle, the Union commander sent most of his cavalry under George Stoneman on a raid toward Richmond, which left him with little information about the enemy’s movements.
tossups.r: That commander, Joseph Hooker, was then surprised by Stonewall Jackson’s flank attack. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia.

tossups.p: Before this battle, a Union general reportedly boasted that his plans were perfect and “may God have mercy on General Lee, for I will have none.” That general marched most of his army across the Rappahannock and Rapidan Rivers to get behind Lee, then pulled back to defend.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in which Joseph Hooker lost to Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson.

tossups.p: According to the journalist Noah Brooks, Abraham Lincoln paced the room after hearing the news of this battle, crying out, “My God! My God! What will the country say?” The defeated Union army had outnumbered its enemy by more than two to one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 Union defeat, in which Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded by his own men.

tossups.p: Cavalry general Jeb Stuart temporarily led an infantry corps on May 3, 1863, during this battle, after its commander was wounded and the next general in line, A. P. Hill, was also hurt.
tossups.r: The wounded commander was Stonewall Jackson, who died on May 10. For 10 points, name this battle in which Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle fought without James Longstreet, who had taken two divisions to gather supplies near Suffolk in southeastern Virginia. Even so, that general split his outnumbered army twice during this battle and won.
tossups.r: That general was Robert E. Lee. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Lee beat Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: Historians usually identify this battle as the one that Stephen Crane’s novel _The Red Badge of Courage_ never names, in which the young soldier Henry Fleming runs from the fighting and later returns to his regiment.
tossups.r: In real life, this battle was a victory for Robert E. Lee, though Stonewall Jackson was shot by his own men. For 10 points, name this 1863 battle.

tossups.p: The losing general in this battle disliked his nickname, “Fighting Joe,” which came from a newspaper headline that left out a dash. Months before this battle, Abraham Lincoln’s letter giving him command warned, “What I now ask of you is military success, and I will risk the dictatorship.”
tossups.r: That general was Joseph Hooker. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in which Hooker lost to Robert E. Lee.

tossups.p: Late on the afternoon of May 2, 1863, during this battle, deer and rabbits burst out of the woods toward Union soldiers, many of whom were cooking supper. Moments later, thousands of enemy troops came charging out of the trees behind the animals.
tossups.r: That surprise attack by Stonewall Jackson routed Oliver O. Howard’s XI Corps. For 10 points, name this battle, Robert E. Lee’s greatest victory.

tossups.p: This battle’s site is one of four battlefields preserved in the Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park. It was named for a large brick house and inn at a crossroads in a scrubby forest called the Wilderness, not for a town.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle in Virginia, where Robert E. Lee defeated Joseph Hooker.

tossups.p: Historians often call this battle Robert E. Lee’s “perfect battle,” though he lost more than one-fifth of his army in it. Afterward, Lee marched north toward Pennsylvania, and George Meade replaced the losing Union commander just days before the armies met again.
tossups.r: That next meeting came at Gettysburg. For 10 points, name this May 1863 battle where Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded.

trap.title: Chancellorsville or the Wilderness?
trap.body: Chancellorsville (May 1863) and the Battle of the Wilderness (May 1864) were fought in the same tangled Virginia forest, a year apart. Chancellorsville was Lee’s win over Joseph Hooker, where Stonewall Jackson was shot; the Wilderness was Lee against Ulysses S. Grant. The first Battle of Fredericksburg (December 1862) was fought just a few miles east, and Gettysburg came two months after Chancellorsville.
trap.fix: Hooker, Jackson’s flank march, and Jackson’s death mean Chancellorsville. Grant and 1864 mean the Wilderness; Ambrose Burnside’s failed charges in December 1862 mean Fredericksburg.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Chancellorsville (do not accept “Battle of the Wilderness” or “Fredericksburg”)

topics.name: Battle of Iwo Jima
topics.kicker: 1945 Marine battle south of Japan · Flag raising on Mount Suribachi
topics.briefing: Iwo Jima, a tiny volcanic island south of Japan that Japan renamed Iōtō in 2007, is covered in black sand and smells of sulfur. In February 1945, U.S. Marines landed to capture its airfields, and on the fifth day Joe Rosenthal photographed six men raising an American flag on Mount Suribachi, one of the most famous photos ever taken. The battle lasted more than a month; nearly 7,000 Americans and almost all of about 21,000 Japanese defenders died.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of Iwo Jima (or Operation Detachment; accept Iōtō; prompt on Mount Suribachi; do not accept “Okinawa”)
reject: raising the flag on iwo jima

tossups.p: Staff Sergeant Louis Lowery of _Leatherneck_ magazine photographed an earlier, smaller version of this battle’s most famous moment, but his pictures were overshadowed by ones taken a few hours later on the same summit.
tossups.r: Those later pictures, by Joe Rosenthal, show Marines raising a large flag on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Marine cameraman Bill Genaust shot color film of this battle’s most famous moment while standing just a few feet from a photographer whose still picture of it became famous. Genaust was killed in the fighting days later, and his body was never found.
tossups.r: That photographer, Joe Rosenthal, won a Pulitzer Prize for his picture of a flag raising on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Navy Secretary James Forrestal came ashore during this battle with Lieutenant General Holland Smith and reportedly told him that a sight on a nearby mountaintop meant “a Marine Corps for the next five hundred years.”
tossups.r: That sight was a U.S. flag flying over Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle on a volcanic island south of Japan.

tossups.p: Sculptor Felix de Weldon worked for years to turn a photograph from this battle into a huge bronze statue, which was dedicated in Arlington, Virginia, on November 10, 1954, the Marine Corps’ birthday. Its base quotes Admiral Chester Nimitz: “Uncommon valor was a common virtue.”
tossups.r: That statue, the Marine Corps War Memorial, shows Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle.

tossups.p: Gunnery Sergeant John Basilone, who had already won the Medal of Honor at Guadalcanal, was killed on the first day of this battle, February 19, 1945, while leading his men inland from the beach.
tossups.r: Four days later, Marines raised a flag atop Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this battle on an island south of Japan.

tossups.p: Johnny Cash recorded a 1964 ballad about Ira Hayes, a Pima [“PEE-muh”] Marine from Arizona who came home a hero after this battle but struggled for the rest of his short life.
tossups.r: Hayes was one of the men in Joe Rosenthal’s photo of a flag raising in this battle. For 10 points, name this 1945 battle.

tossups.p: James Bradley’s book _Flags of Our Fathers_ is about his father, a Navy medical corpsman long believed to appear in a famous photo from this battle. Clint Eastwood turned that book into a 2006 film and made a companion film the same year about the Japanese defenders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle, where Marines raised the U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi in February 1945.

tossups.p: Japanese general Tadamichi Kuribayashi [“koo-ree-bah-YAH-shee”] had his troops dig miles of tunnels and hidden bunkers before this battle, and he ordered them not to waste their lives in mass charges. Nearly all of his roughly 21,000 men died.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1945 battle in which U.S. Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: After this battle, P-51 Mustang fighters flying from its island escorted B-29 bombers on raids over Japan, and thousands of crewmen in damaged B-29s made emergency landings on its airfields.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, famous for a photo of Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: A Marine signal officer said that the Marines would never have taken this battle’s island without the Navajo code talkers; six of them sent more than 800 messages without an error during its first two days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1945 battle in which Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: Twenty-seven Medals of Honor were awarded for actions in this battle, and Admiral Chester Nimitz said that among the Americans who served there, “uncommon valor was a common virtue.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle that began on February 19, 1945, and is remembered for a flag raising on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: This battle’s island is part of Japan’s Volcano Islands, about 750 miles south of Tokyo, and its name means “Sulfur Island.” Its soft black volcanic sand made it hard for Marines to dig foxholes or move vehicles off the beaches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, famous for a photo of Marines raising a flag on Mount Suribachi.

tossups.p: Marine commanders asked for ten days of naval shelling before this battle but received only three, so most of the enemy’s hidden guns survived to fire on the landing beaches.
tossups.r: Marines came ashore on February 19, 1945. For 10 points, name this battle, where a famous photo showed Marines raising a flag.

tossups.p: Major General Harry Schmidt led the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Marine Divisions of the V Amphibious Corps in this battle, which lasted more than a month on an island of only about eight square miles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle, fought from February to March 1945, whose flag raising inspired the Marine Corps War Memorial.

tossups.p: John Wayne earned an Oscar nomination for playing a tough sergeant in a 1949 film about this battle, in which three men then believed to be in a famous photograph from it made brief appearances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this February 1945 battle, where Marines raised a flag on Mount Suribachi.

trap.title: Iwo Jima or Okinawa?
trap.body: The two biggest Marine battles of 1945 are easy to mix up. Iwo Jima (February–March 1945) was a small volcanic island captured for its airfields, with the famous flag raising on Mount Suribachi. Okinawa (April–June 1945) was a much larger island and the last major battle of the Pacific war, where kamikaze planes attacked U.S. ships.
trap.fix: Suribachi, Rosenthal’s photo, Kuribayashi, black volcanic sand, and B-29 emergency landings mean Iwo Jima; kamikazes and an April 1945 invasion mean Okinawa. Saying “Mount Suribachi” alone earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of Iwo Jima (or Operation Detachment; accept Iōtō; prompt on Mount Suribachi; do not accept “Okinawa”)

topics.name: Battles of Lexington and Concord
topics.kicker: First battles of the Revolution, 1775 · “The shot heard round the world”
topics.briefing: On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out of Boston to warn that British troops were marching to seize the colonists’ gunpowder and weapons. At dawn the next day, shots rang out on the town green at Lexington, and later that morning militiamen drove the British back at Concord’s North Bridge, firing Emerson’s famous “shot heard round the world.” The redcoats retreated to Boston under fire, and the American Revolution had begun.
topics.answerHtml: Battles of Lexington and Concord (accept either underlined part; prompt on North Bridge; do not accept “Bunker Hill”)
accept: the battles of lexington and concord

tossups.p: Prince Estabrook, an enslaved Black man serving in Captain John Parker’s militia company, was wounded in the first clash of this pair of battles. That clash took place around sunrise on a town green, where eight militiamen were killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, that began the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Captain Isaac Davis of Acton was killed leading his company toward a bridge during this pair of battles, and Major John Buttrick then ordered the militia to return fire. The British soldiers guarding the bridge soon fell back toward the town.
tossups.r: Ralph Waldo Emerson called that volley “the shot heard round the world.” For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Daniel Chester French, who later designed the seated statue in the Lincoln Memorial, made his first major work, a farmer-soldier holding a musket beside a plow, for the 100th anniversary of this pair of battles in 1875.
tossups.r: That statue, _The Minute Man_, stands near the North Bridge. For 10 points, name these battles that began the Revolution in April 1775.

tossups.p: At the dedication of a battle monument on July 4, 1837, townspeople sang a hymn by a local writer whose grandfather had been the town’s minister in 1775. That hymn says the “embattled farmers” stood by “the rude bridge that arched the flood.”
tossups.r: Its writer, Ralph Waldo Emerson, called their first volley “the shot heard round the world.” For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Lord Hugh Percy led about 1,000 British reinforcements out of Boston during this pair of battles, bringing cannons to rescue an exhausted column that was retreating under fire. Percy’s men met that column in the early afternoon, near the site of the morning’s first shots.
tossups.r: Afterward, militiamen surrounded Boston, beginning a long siege. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, the first fighting of the American Revolution.

tossups.p: On the night before this pair of battles, two men quietly rowed a silversmith across the Charles River, past the British warship HMS _Somerset_. In Charlestown, the silversmith borrowed a horse and rode off to spread the alarm.
tossups.r: That rider was Paul Revere, sent by Dr. Joseph Warren. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that started the American Revolution.

tossups.p: Sexton Robert Newman climbed a church steeple on the night before this pair of battles to hang a signal meant for patriots across the river in Charlestown, in case the man who arranged it was caught.
tossups.r: That signal was two lanterns in Boston’s Old North Church, meaning the British were crossing by water. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith commanded the British troops sent out during this pair of battles, and Major John Pitcairn of the Royal Marines led the advance companies that met the first militiamen.
tossups.r: General Thomas Gage had sent those troops to seize colonial weapons and gunpowder. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775.

tossups.p: Words carved on a boulder at the site of this pair of battles’ first clash, credited to a militia captain, read: “Stand your ground. Don’t fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here.”
tossups.r: That captain was John Parker. For 10 points, name these battles of April 19, 1775, in which minutemen faced British redcoats.

tossups.p: British soldiers searched Colonel James Barrett’s farm for hidden cannons during this pair of battles. When smoke rose from the town where soldiers were burning captured supplies, militiamen on a nearby hill feared the town was on fire and marched toward a bridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles in Massachusetts, where Emerson’s “shot heard round the world” was fired.

tossups.p: During the night before this pair of battles, a British patrol captured a famous rider near the town of Lincoln, but Samuel Prescott, a young doctor riding with him, jumped his horse over a stone wall and escaped.
tossups.r: Prescott carried the alarm on to the second town, which Paul Revere never reached. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Samuel Adams and John Hancock were staying at minister Jonas Clarke’s house when riders arrived around midnight to warn them, hours before this pair of battles began. One rider had taken the long way out of Boston, over the narrow neck of land, while the other crossed the river by boat.
tossups.r: Those riders were Paul Revere and William Dawes. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that began the Revolutionary War.

tossups.p: Fighting broke out again at Meriam’s Corner during this pair of battles, as militiamen from many towns fired from behind stone walls, trees, and houses at a column marching back toward Boston.
tossups.r: By nightfall, more than 70 British soldiers and about 50 colonists had been killed. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles.

tossups.p: Massachusetts and Maine honor this pair of battles with a state holiday on the third Monday in April, the same day the Boston Marathon is run. Reenactors gather on a town green at dawn that day to recreate the first shots.
tossups.r: That holiday is Patriots’ Day. For 10 points, name these battles fought on April 19, 1775.

tossups.p: Historians say a famous rider before this pair of battles probably warned that “the Regulars are coming out,” not that “the British are coming,” since most colonists still thought of themselves as British. A Henry Wadsworth Longfellow poem later made that rider a national hero.
tossups.r: That rider was Paul Revere. For 10 points, name these April 1775 battles that began the American Revolution.

trap.title: Not Bunker Hill!
trap.body: These battles happened in two towns on one day, April 19, 1775: the first shots came at dawn on the town green in Lexington, and Emerson’s “shot heard round the world” came later that morning at the North Bridge in Concord. Bunker Hill was a separate, bigger battle two months later, in June 1775. And Paul Revere never reached Concord: a British patrol captured him, and Samuel Prescott carried the warning the rest of the way.
trap.fix: Revere and Dawes, the two lanterns, John Parker, the North Bridge, and Patriots’ Day mean Lexington and Concord. “The whites of their eyes,” Breed’s Hill, and William Howe mean Bunker Hill. This answer line accepts either town alone.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battles of Lexington and Concord (accept either underlined part; prompt on North Bridge; do not accept “Bunker Hill”)

topics.name: Battle of San Jacinto
topics.kicker: Sam Houston’s 18-minute victory, 1836 · Won independence for Texas
topics.briefing: On the afternoon of April 21, 1836, Sam Houston’s ragged Texian army charged across an open field into Santa Anna’s Mexican camp, shouting “Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!” The surprise attack was over in about 18 minutes. The next day, Texians captured Santa Anna, who was hiding in a common soldier’s clothes, and Texas won its independence from Mexico.
topics.answerHtml: Battle of San Jacinto (prompt on Texas Revolution; do not accept “Alamo” or “Goliad”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Shortly before this battle, scout Erastus “Deaf” Smith and his men destroyed Vince’s Bridge, cutting off a route that either army might have used to escape or to bring in more troops.
tossups.r: Hours later, Sam Houston’s army attacked and defeated Santa Anna. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle that won Texas its independence.

tossups.p: As the Texian army advanced in this battle, a fife and drum played a popular love song, “Will You Come to the Bower?” A low rise in the prairie hid the advancing soldiers until they were close to the enemy camp.
tossups.r: Shouting “Remember the Alamo!” they routed Santa Anna’s army in about 18 minutes. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle.

tossups.p: A private named Mirabeau Lamar [“MEER-uh-boh luh-MAR”] rescued Secretary of War Thomas Rusk during a skirmish the day before this battle, and he was promoted to colonel to lead the cavalry in it. Lamar later became the second president of the Republic of Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna on April 21, 1836.

tossups.p: Juan Seguín [“seh-GEEN”], who later served as mayor of San Antonio, led a company of Tejano soldiers on the Texian side in this battle. Weeks earlier, he had left the Alamo as a messenger seeking help.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where Sam Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna and won independence for Texas.

tossups.p: William Henry Huddle’s 1886 painting of the day after this battle, which hangs in the Texas Capitol, shows a wounded general lying under an oak tree as a captured enemy leader is brought before him.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle where Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: On the morning of this battle, General Martín Perfecto de Cos [“KOHSS”] arrived with about 500 Mexican reinforcements, many of them tired from a long march. That afternoon, the Texians attacked the enlarged camp.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Sam Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna in about 18 minutes.

tossups.p: Citizens of Cincinnati, Ohio, paid for two small cannons that were shipped to the Texian army before this battle. Those cannons, nicknamed the “Twin Sisters,” fired on the enemy during this battle, and what became of them after the Civil War is a mystery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle where Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna and won Texas its independence.

tossups.p: Starting in 1948, the battleship USS _Texas_ was docked for decades beside the site of this battle, near a 567-foot monument topped by a giant star. That monument, finished in 1939, is taller than the Washington Monument.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1836 battle near present-day Houston, where Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: A legend that historians doubt claims that Emily West, a free Black woman in the Mexican camp, distracted the enemy general just before this battle and inspired the song “The Yellow Rose of Texas.”
tossups.r: In this battle, Sam Houston’s army shouted “Remember the Alamo!” For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle that ended the Texas Revolution.

tossups.p: After this battle, Vicente Filisola [“fee-lee-SOH-lah”] led most of the remaining Mexican army back toward the Rio Grande, obeying orders sent by his captured commander. Filisola, an Italian-born general, had been second-in-command of the Mexican army in Texas.
tossups.r: That commander, Santa Anna, later signed the Treaties of Velasco [“veh-LAHS-koh”]. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle that won independence for Texas.

tossups.p: Before this battle, the winning army spent about two weeks drilling at Groce’s plantation on the Brazos River, while frightened settlers fled east in the panic called the “Runaway Scrape.” Some of its officers grumbled that their commander would never stand and fight.
tossups.r: Sam Houston then turned and attacked Santa Anna. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle had a horse shot out from under him and was wounded in the ankle by a musket ball, but he stayed in command until the fighting ended. Weeks later, he sailed to New Orleans for treatment.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this battle where Houston’s army defeated Santa Anna in about 18 minutes.

tossups.p: Months after this battle, the losing general traveled to Washington, D.C., where he met President Andrew Jackson in January 1837. As a prisoner, he had signed treaties promising to pull his troops back beyond the Rio Grande.
tossups.r: Texians had captured that general, Santa Anna, the day after this battle. For 10 points, name this April 1836 battle.

tossups.p: Augustus and John Allen founded a town on Buffalo Bayou months after this battle and named it for the battle’s winning general, who soon became the first elected president of the Republic of Texas.
tossups.r: That general was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this 1836 battle where Houston defeated Santa Anna.

tossups.p: This battle took place on a plain where Buffalo Bayou meets a river, near present-day La Porte, Texas. The attack came late in the afternoon, catching the enemy camp off guard while many soldiers rested.
tossups.r: The fighting lasted about 18 minutes. For 10 points, name this April 21, 1836, battle that won independence for Texas.

trap.title: Battle cry, not answer
trap.body: Tossups about this battle often mention the Alamo and Goliad, because Texian soldiers shouted “Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!” as they charged. A player who hears “Alamo” and blurts it out loses the question: the Alamo (February–March 1836) and Goliad (March 1836) were Texian defeats, while this battle on April 21, 1836, was the victory that won independence.
trap.fix: Sam Houston’s surprise attack, an 18-minute battle, the Twin Sisters cannons, and Santa Anna’s capture the next day mean San Jacinto. “Remember the Alamo” is the battle cry shouted here, not the answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of San Jacinto (prompt on Texas Revolution; do not accept “Alamo” or “Goliad”)

topics.name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
topics.kicker: Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho defeat Custer’s 7th Cavalry · Montana, June 1876
topics.briefing: On June 25, 1876, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led the U.S. 7th Cavalry in an attack on a huge camp of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho people beside Montana’s Little Bighorn River. Warriors led by Crazy Horse, Gall, and others won a major victory, and Custer and every soldier in the five companies he led were killed. The Lakota and Cheyenne call it the Battle of the Greasy Grass; it is also known as “Custer’s Last Stand.”
topics.answerHtml: Battle of the Little Bighorn (accept Battle of the Greasy Grass or Custer’s Last Stand; prompt on Bighorn or Great Sioux War; do not accept “Wounded Knee”)
accept: battle of the little big horn

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In early June 1876, a Hunkpapa [“HUNK-pah-pah”] Lakota holy man took part in a Sun Dance and saw a vision of soldiers falling upside down into his people’s camp. About three weeks later, cavalry soldiers attacked that camp, beside a river in Montana, in this battle.
tossups.r: That holy man was Sitting Bull. For 10 points, name this battle in which Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer.

tossups.p: Mark Kellogg, a newspaper reporter for the _Bismarck Tribune_, was killed while riding with the soldiers in this battle. Word of this battle reached the eastern states in early July 1876, during celebrations of the nation’s 100th birthday.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1876 battle in Montana, where George Armstrong Custer and every soldier in his five companies were killed.

tossups.p: After a grass fire swept across this battle’s site in 1983, archaeologists mapped bullets and cartridge cases left on the ground. Their work showed that many of the Native fighters here had repeating rifles, while the soldiers carried single-shot carbines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1876 battle in which Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer’s troops.

tossups.p: Before this battle, one officer turned down an offer of Gatling guns because he thought they would slow his troops down. His regiment belonged to General Alfred Terry’s column, one of three Army forces sent in 1876 to force Lakota and Cheyenne bands onto reservations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in Montana where that officer, George Armstrong Custer, was killed along with every soldier in his five companies.

tossups.p: In 1879, Major Marcus Reno asked for a court of inquiry to answer critics who blamed him for this battle’s outcome. Reno had attacked the south end of a huge village, then retreated across the river to a hilltop.
tossups.r: Most of the soldiers with Reno and Frederick Benteen survived there. For 10 points, name this battle in which their commander, George Armstrong Custer, was killed.

tossups.p: Bloody Knife, an Arikara [“uh-RIK-uh-ruh”] scout who was a longtime favorite of the commanding officer, was killed early in this battle during Major Marcus Reno’s attack on the village. Scouts had warned that the camp ahead was enormous.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1876 battle in which warriors led by Crazy Horse and Gall defeated George Armstrong Custer.

tossups.p: Captain Myles Keogh [“KEE-oh”] was killed with his entire company in this battle, but his badly wounded horse survived. The 7th Cavalry later ordered that the horse, Comanche, should never be ridden again, and it became a living symbol of this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle where George Armstrong Custer and his 7th Cavalry were defeated in June 1876.

tossups.p: Captain Grant Marsh’s steamboat, the _Far West_, rushed wounded soldiers from this battle down the Yellowstone and Missouri Rivers to Bismarck in record time. Those soldiers had survived with Major Marcus Reno and Captain Frederick Benteen on a hilltop above the river.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1876 battle in which George Armstrong Custer and every soldier in his five companies were killed.

tossups.p: Two Moons led Northern Cheyenne warriors in this battle, and the Cheyenne leader Lame White Man was among the Native fighters killed in it. The warriors came from a camp of several thousand people that stretched along a river valley in Montana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry in June 1876.

tossups.p: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote about this battle in the poem “The Revenge of Rain-in-the-Face.” Within weeks of this battle, Walt Whitman published a poem honoring the commander who died in it, which he later retitled “From Far Dakota’s Cañons.”
tossups.r: That commander’s body was found on a ridge now called Last Stand Hill. For 10 points, name this 1876 battle where Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer.

tossups.p: In Thomas Berger’s novel _Little Big Man_, the narrator Jack Crabb claims to be the only white survivor of this battle, and Dustin Hoffman played Crabb in the 1970 film version. An earlier film, _They Died with Their Boots On_, climaxes with this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1876 battle in Montana where George Armstrong Custer was killed along with every soldier in his five companies.

tossups.p: In 1991, Congress renamed the national monument at this battle’s site, which had been named for the U.S. officer killed there. In 2003, an Indian Memorial was dedicated nearby to honor the Native people who took part in this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in which the Lakota leaders Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse won their most famous victory, over George Armstrong Custer.

tossups.p: Eight days before this battle, warriors led by Crazy Horse fought General George Crook’s soldiers to a standstill at Rosebud Creek, so Crook’s column was not there to help. The camp then moved west to a river valley in Montana Territory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1876 battle where George Armstrong Custer and every soldier in his five companies were killed.

tossups.p: After gold was found in the Black Hills, land promised to the Lakota by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, the government ordered all Lakota bands to report to reservations by January 31, 1876. Many bands that ignored the order gathered in the huge camp attacked in this battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1876 battle in which Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer.

tossups.p: During this battle, trumpeter John Martin carried a hurried note from adjutant William Cooke to Captain Frederick Benteen: “Come on. Big village. Be quick. Bring packs.” Benteen instead joined Major Marcus Reno’s soldiers on a hilltop, where most of them survived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this June 1876 battle where George Armstrong Custer and all the men with him were killed.

Custer split his regiment: Major Marcus Reno attacked the south end of the village, and Captain Frederick Benteen scouted the hills to the south
Reno’s men retreated across the river to a hilltop, where Benteen joined them; most of their soldiers survived

Weeks earlier, Sitting Bull had a vision at a Sun Dance of soldiers falling upside down into the camp

trap.title: Battle, man, or massacre?
trap.body: Little Bighorn questions are full of names that are answer lines of their own: George Armstrong Custer (the commander who died), Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse (Lakota leaders), and the Battle of the Rosebud (Crazy Horse’s fight with George Crook eight days earlier). The Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) involved the same 7th Cavalry regiment but happened 14 years later, in South Dakota.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this battle” wants the Little Bighorn, while “this man” or “this commander” wants Custer. Answer lines also accept the Lakota and Cheyenne name, the Battle of the Greasy Grass, and “Custer’s Last Stand.” December 1890, the Ghost Dance, and Spotted Elk (Big Foot) mean Wounded Knee.
trap.line: Real answer line: Battle of the Little Bighorn (accept Battle of the Greasy Grass or Custer’s Last Stand; prompt on Bighorn or Great Sioux War; do not accept “Wounded Knee”)

topics.name: Ben Bernanke
topics.kicker: Federal Reserve chair, 2006–2014 · Steered the Fed through the 2008 crisis
topics.briefing: As a boy in Dillon, South Carolina, Ben Bernanke made it to the National Spelling Bee; he grew up to be an economist who studied why the Great Depression was so severe. He chaired the Federal Reserve, America’s central bank, from 2006 to 2014, steering it through the financial crisis of 2008. _Time_ named him Person of the Year for 2009, and in 2022 he shared the Nobel Prize in economics for research on banks and financial crises.
topics.answerHtml: Ben Bernanke (accept Benjamin Shalom Bernanke; prompt on Helicopter Ben)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At age 11, this future economist represented South Carolina at the 1965 National Spelling Bee, where he was knocked out on the word “edelweiss.” He grew up in the small town of Dillon, where his father was a pharmacist.
tossups.r: He later led the Fed through the 2008 financial crisis. For 10 points, name this man who chaired the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man spent summers waiting tables at South of the Border, a roadside stop near his South Carolina hometown. He later earned a Ph.D. at MIT, where Stanley Fischer advised him, after graduating from Harvard.
tossups.r: He taught at Princeton before joining the Fed. For 10 points, name this economist who led the Federal Reserve during the 2008 financial crisis.

tossups.p: This economist’s 1983 paper argued that waves of bank failures made the Great Depression worse by cutting off credit to households and small businesses. He collected his research on that era in the book _Essays on the Great Depression_.
tossups.r: That research helped win him a 2022 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this Princeton professor who chaired the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: At a 2002 conference honoring Milton Friedman’s 90th birthday, this man told Friedman and Anna Schwartz that they were right about the central bank’s role in the Great Depression, saying, “We did it. We’re very sorry.”
tossups.r: He was then a member of the Federal Reserve Board. For 10 points, name this economist who chaired the Fed from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: In a 2004 speech, this economist described the “Great Moderation,” a long period of steady growth and mild inflation after the mid-1980s. Two years earlier, a speech on fighting deflation, in which he mentioned Milton Friedman’s idea of a “helicopter drop” of money, had earned him a nickname.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man nicknamed “Helicopter Ben,” who chaired the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: In 2005, this economist argued that a “global saving glut,” as countries like China saved huge sums, was helping keep U.S. interest rates low. That year, he became chairman of President George W. Bush’s Council of Economic Advisers.
tossups.r: Bush then chose him to lead the Federal Reserve. For 10 points, name this successor to Alan Greenspan.

tossups.p: In March 2008, this man’s agency helped JPMorgan Chase buy the failing investment bank Bear Stearns. Six months later, Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, but his agency made an emergency loan to the insurance giant AIG.
tossups.r: That December, his agency cut short-term interest rates to nearly zero. For 10 points, name this Federal Reserve chair during the 2008 financial crisis.

tossups.p: This man co-wrote the 2019 book _Firefighting_ with Timothy Geithner and Henry Paulson. Eleven years earlier, he and Treasury Secretary Paulson had urged Congress to pass the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program to steady the banking system.
tossups.r: He had succeeded Alan Greenspan in 2006. For 10 points, name this man who chaired the Federal Reserve during the 2008 financial crisis.

tossups.p: In 2012, this man’s agency set an official inflation goal of 2 percent for the first time. Starting in late 2008, it had bought huge amounts of bonds in a program called “quantitative easing,” meant to push down long-term interest rates.
tossups.r: He had earlier taught economics at Princeton. For 10 points, name this Federal Reserve chair from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: In April 2011, this man became the first head of his agency to hold regular press conferences after its policy meetings. Two years later, his hint that the agency would slow its bond buying set off the “taper tantrum” in markets.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Federal Reserve chair who was succeeded by Janet Yellen in 2014.

tossups.p: This economist co-wrote the college textbook _Principles of Economics_ with Robert Frank. His 2015 memoir, _The Courage to Act_, describes leading a central bank through a financial panic, a job he left in 2014 to join the Brookings Institution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economist who succeeded Alan Greenspan as chair of the Federal Reserve.

tossups.p: This economist shared a 2022 prize with Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig, whose 1983 model showed how fear can set off a run on a bank. The prize committee praised his research on bank failures during the Great Depression.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this winner of the Nobel Prize in economics who chaired the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014.

tossups.p: In August 2009, Barack Obama announced that he would reappoint this man, who had first been chosen for his post by George W. Bush. Months later, _Time_ magazine named him its Person of the Year for 2009.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economist who chaired the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014, succeeding Alan Greenspan.

tossups.p: As a professor, this economist co-wrote a book on inflation targeting, in which a central bank announces a clear goal for inflation. In 2009, his agency led “stress tests” of the 19 largest U.S. banks to see whether they could survive an even deeper recession.
tossups.r: He served from 2006 to 2014. For 10 points, name this Federal Reserve chair during the Great Recession.

tossups.p: In 2011, this man’s agency launched a bond-swapping program nicknamed “Operation Twist,” borrowing the name of a similar 1961 program. Its goal was to lower long-term interest rates and help the slow recovery from the Great Recession.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economist who chaired the Federal Reserve between Alan Greenspan and Janet Yellen.

trap.title: Which Fed chair?
trap.body: Federal Reserve chairs come up often, and their clues overlap. Alan Greenspan led the Fed from 1987 to 2006, just before this economist; Janet Yellen followed him in 2014 as the first woman to chair the Fed; and Paul Volcker fought high inflation around 1980. Henry Paulson was the Treasury Secretary, not a Fed chair, during the 2008 crisis.
trap.fix: Great Depression research, Princeton, “Helicopter Ben,” the 2008 crisis, and the 2022 Nobel Prize mean Bernanke. Greenspan clues include the 1987 stock market crash and “irrational exuberance”; Yellen clues include being the first woman to chair the Fed and later serving as Treasury Secretary (2021–2025).
trap.line: Real answer line: Ben Bernanke (accept Benjamin Shalom Bernanke; prompt on Helicopter Ben)

topics.name: Billy the Kid
topics.kicker: Outlaw of the Lincoln County War · Killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881
topics.briefing: Billy the Kid was born Henry McCarty, probably in New York City, and also went by Henry Antrim and William H. Bonney. As a teenager in New Mexico Territory, he joined one side of a deadly feud called the Lincoln County War and became a wanted outlaw. Sheriff Pat Garrett captured him in 1880; after Billy escaped from jail, killing two deputies, Garrett tracked him down and shot him at Fort Sumner on July 14, 1881.
topics.answerHtml: Billy the Kid (accept Henry McCarty, William H. Bonney, or Henry Antrim; prompt on Kid or Billy)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a teenager in Silver City, New Mexico Territory, this future outlaw was jailed for holding a bundle of stolen laundry, and he escaped by climbing up the jail’s chimney. His mother had died of tuberculosis there the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw who was shot and killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In 1877, near Camp Grant in Arizona Territory, this young man shot and killed a blacksmith named Frank “Windy” Cahill during a fight, then fled to New Mexico. There he later went to work for the English rancher John Tunstall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War who was later killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: This young ranch hand joined a group called the Regulators after a sheriff’s posse killed his employer, John Tunstall, in February 1878. Tunstall and the lawyer Alexander McSween had challenged the business owners known as “the House,” led by James Dolan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw who fought in the resulting Lincoln County War and was later killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: On April 1, 1878, Sheriff William Brady was killed in an ambush on the main street of Lincoln by a group of gunmen that included this man. Three years later, a court in Mesilla [“meh-SEE-yuh”] convicted this man of Brady’s murder and sentenced him to hang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War, later killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: In July 1878, this man was among the fighters trapped inside Alexander McSween’s house during a five-day gun battle in the town of Lincoln. When the house was set on fire, he escaped into the night, but McSween was killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this young outlaw of the Lincoln County War who was later hunted down by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: In March 1879, this man met secretly with a territorial governor who was then writing the novel _Ben-Hur_. He agreed to testify about the killing of the lawyer Huston Chapman in exchange for a pardon, but the pardon never came.
tossups.r: That governor was Lew Wallace. For 10 points, name this outlaw who was killed by Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In December 1880, Governor Lew Wallace offered a $500 reward for this outlaw’s capture. That same month, a posse surrounded this man’s gang in a small stone building at Stinking Springs, killed Charlie Bowdre, and forced the rest to surrender.
tossups.r: That posse was led by Sheriff Pat Garrett. For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Garrett later killed.

tossups.p: On April 28, 1881, this prisoner, who was awaiting execution, escaped from the Lincoln County courthouse after killing his two guards, deputies James Bell and Robert Olinger. He rode away and returned to his friends near Fort Sumner.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Pat Garrett tracked down and killed less than three months later.

tossups.p: This man’s last words, spoken in a darkened bedroom at Fort Sumner, are usually given as “¿Quién es?” (Spanish for “Who is it?”). That bedroom belonged to Pete Maxwell, whom a sheriff had come to question about this man’s whereabouts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw shot and killed by Pat Garrett on July 14, 1881.

tossups.p: This man is buried at Fort Sumner beside two friends, Tom O’Folliard and Charlie Bowdre, under a shared stone marked “Pals.” His own gravestone has been stolen more than once, and the graves are protected by a metal cage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881, when he was about 21.

tossups.p: In 2011, a tintype photograph of this man taken around 1880 sold at auction for $2.3 million. Because tintypes show a mirror image, people long believed he was left-handed, an idea used in the title of a 1958 Paul Newman film.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War, killed by Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In 1882, a sheriff published a book about this man that was largely ghostwritten by the sheriff’s friend Ash Upson and helped spread many legends. One legend claimed this man had killed 21 men, one for each year of his life, though historians count far fewer.
tossups.r: That sheriff was Pat Garrett. For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Garrett had killed the year before.

tossups.p: In 1950, a Texas man named Brushy Bill Roberts claimed to be this outlaw, saying he had survived and lived for decades under another name. In 2010, New Mexico governor Bill Richardson decided not to grant this outlaw a pardon that had been promised long before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Sheriff Pat Garrett killed at Fort Sumner in 1881.

tossups.p: Eugene Loring created the dances for a 1938 ballet about this outlaw for Lincoln Kirstein’s company, Ballet Caravan. That ballet’s score quotes cowboy songs and includes a section called “Gun Battle.” It begins and ends with music picturing the open prairie.
tossups.r: Its composer was Aaron Copland. For 10 points, name this outlaw who was killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: Emilio Estevez played this outlaw in the 1988 film _Young Guns_, and Kris Kristofferson played him in a 1973 Sam Peckinpah Western whose soundtrack, by Bob Dylan, includes “Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door.” A ballad about him appears on _Piano Man_, an album released that same year.

trap.title: Which name? Which Kid?
trap.body: This outlaw used several names: he was born Henry McCarty, went by Henry Antrim (his stepfather’s last name) as a teenager, and later called himself William H. Bonney. Answer lines accept all of them. Don’t confuse him with other Western “Kids,” like the Sundance Kid (Butch Cassidy’s partner) or the made-up Cisco Kid, or with Pat Garrett, the sheriff who killed him.
trap.fix: Lincoln County, John Tunstall, Lew Wallace, Fort Sumner, and Pat Garrett mean Billy the Kid. The Sundance Kid robbed trains with Butch Cassidy’s Wild Bunch and is believed to have died in Bolivia. If the question asks for “this sheriff” or “this lawman,” the answer is Pat Garrett.
trap.line: Real answer line: Billy the Kid (accept Henry McCarty, William H. Bonney, or Henry Antrim; prompt on Kid or Billy)

topics.name: Birmingham, Alabama
topics.kicker: Iron and steel city in Alabama · Site of the 1963 civil rights campaign
topics.briefing: Birmingham, Alabama, was founded in 1871 where two railroads crossed near deposits of iron ore, coal, and limestone, and it grew so fast into a steel-making center that it was nicknamed the “Magic City.” In 1963, it became the scene of a major civil rights campaign, when police dogs and fire hoses were turned on young marchers and Martin Luther King Jr. wrote a letter from its jail. That September, a bomb planted by Ku Klux Klan members at the 16th Street Baptist Church killed four Black girls.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Giuseppe Moretti designed a cast-iron statue of the Roman god of the forge for the 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis to show off this city’s iron industry. That statue of Vulcan, the largest cast-iron statue in the world, stands on Red Mountain overlooking this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where Martin Luther King Jr. wrote a famous letter from jail in 1963.

tossups.p: Sloss Furnaces, which made iron from 1882 until 1971, has become a museum in this city. In 1907, U.S. Steel took over the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company, a giant steel company based in this city.
tossups.r: This city grew up around coal, iron ore, and limestone mined nearby. For 10 points, name this Alabama city nicknamed the “Pittsburgh of the South.”

tossups.p: This city was founded in 1871 at the spot where two railroads crossed, and it was named after an industrial city in England. It grew so quickly that people nicknamed it the “Magic City.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this steel-making center in Alabama where civil rights marchers faced fire hoses and police dogs in 1963.

tossups.p: On Christmas night in 1956, a bomb badly damaged the parsonage of Bethel Baptist Church in this city, but its pastor survived. That pastor, Fred Shuttlesworth, had founded the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights after the state banned the NAACP.
tossups.r: In 1963, Shuttlesworth invited Martin Luther King Jr. to lead protests here. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: On Mother’s Day in 1961, a mob attacked a busload of Freedom Riders at this city’s Trailways station while the city’s police stayed away. Public Safety Commissioner Bull Connor claimed few officers were on duty because it was Mother’s Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where Connor later used fire hoses on civil rights marchers in 1963.

tossups.p: Organizers called this city’s 1963 protest campaign Project C, with the C standing for “confrontation.” On Good Friday that year, police arrested a minister here for leading a march that a court order had banned.
tossups.r: That minister, Martin Luther King Jr., then wrote a famous letter from this city’s jail. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: Eight white clergymen published a statement called “A Call for Unity,” urging Black residents of this city to stop protesting and to wait for the courts. A jailed minister answered them in a letter declaring that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city whose jail gave its name to Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 letter.

tossups.p: James Bevel helped organize a “Children’s Crusade” in this city, in which thousands of students skipped school to march in May 1963. So many young marchers were arrested that the city’s jails quickly filled.
tossups.r: Public Safety Commissioner Bull Connor then turned fire hoses and police dogs on the marchers. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: Kelly Ingram Park, where young protesters gathered in 1963, is part of a national monument in this city that Barack Obama created in 2017. Across the street stand the city’s Civil Rights Institute, opened in 1992, and a famous Baptist church.
tossups.r: A bomb planted by Ku Klux Klan members killed four girls at that church in September 1963. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: Businessman A. G. Gaston’s motel served as headquarters for a 1963 civil rights campaign in this city, and it was bombed that May, a day after the campaign’s leaders announced a deal to desegregate stores. The deal promised to open lunch counters and fitting rooms to Black customers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where Martin Luther King Jr. wrote a letter from jail in 1963.

tossups.p: In 2013, Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carole Robertson, and Denise McNair were honored with the Congressional Gold Medal, fifty years after their deaths in this city. Three of them were fourteen years old, and Denise McNair was eleven.
tossups.r: They were killed when a bomb exploded at the 16th Street Baptist Church. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: In 1977, Robert Chambliss was convicted of a 1963 bombing in this city, and Thomas Blanton Jr. and Bobby Frank Cherry were convicted of the same crime decades later. All three men were members of the Ku Klux Klan.
tossups.r: Their bomb killed four girls at the 16th Street Baptist Church. For 10 points, name this Alabama city.

tossups.p: Dudley Randall’s poem about a tragedy in this city tells of a mother who sends her daughter to church because she thinks it is safer than a freedom march. John Coltrane recorded the jazz piece “Alabama” in response to that same 1963 event.
tossups.r: Spike Lee’s documentary _4 Little Girls_ is about it too. For 10 points, name this Alabama city where a church bombing killed four girls.

tossups.p: In a Christopher Paul Curtis novel, the young narrator Kenny and his family drive from Flint, Michigan, to visit his grandmother in this city in 1963. His parents plan to leave his troublemaking older brother, Byron, there with their strict grandmother.
tossups.r: While they are there, Kenny’s little sister Joetta is nearly caught in a church bombing. For 10 points, name this Alabama city named in the novel’s title.

tossups.p: Willie Mays began his professional career with this city’s Black Barons, who played at Rickwood Field, the oldest professional ballpark in the United States. Condoleezza Rice was born here, and Richard Arrington Jr. became its first Black mayor in 1979.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city, home of the Vulcan statue and the 16th Street Baptist Church.

trap.title: Which Alabama city?
trap.body: Alabama civil rights clues come from several cities. The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956) and Rosa Parks belong to Montgomery, the state capital; the 1965 voting rights march began in Selma; and George Wallace’s “stand in the schoolhouse door” happened in Tuscaloosa. Birmingham owns the 1963 campaign: King’s letter from jail, the Children’s Crusade, Bull Connor’s fire hoses, and the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing.
trap.fix: Listen for 1963, Bull Connor, Fred Shuttlesworth, the Children’s Crusade, and the 16th Street Baptist Church: that is Birmingham. Steel, the “Magic City,” and the Vulcan statue also mean Birmingham. Saying only “Alabama” is wrong when the question asks for “this city.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Birmingham, Alabama (do not accept “Alabama” or “Montgomery”)

topics.name: Camp David Accords
topics.kicker: 1978 Egypt–Israel peace framework · Brokered by Jimmy Carter in Maryland
topics.briefing: For 13 days in September 1978, President Jimmy Carter hosted Egypt’s Anwar Sadat and Israel’s Menachem Begin at Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland’s mountains, and pushed them toward peace. The Camp David Accords led to a 1979 treaty in which Israel agreed to return the Sinai Peninsula and Egypt became the first Arab country to recognize Israel. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize.
topics.answerHtml: Camp David Accords (accept Framework for Peace in the Middle East; prompt on Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty; do not accept “Oslo Accords”)
accept: framework for peace in the middle east

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During the talks that produced these agreements, the host took the other two leaders to tour the Gettysburg battlefield. Those talks lasted thirteen days in September 1978, at a presidential retreat in Maryland’s mountains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements between Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Menachem Begin of Israel, brokered by Jimmy Carter.

tossups.p: On the last day of the talks that produced these agreements, the American president gave one leader signed photographs, each addressed by name to one of that leader’s grandchildren. The gift moved the leader at a moment when the talks seemed close to collapse.
tossups.r: That leader was Menachem Begin of Israel. For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements that Begin made with Anwar Sadat of Egypt.

tossups.p: Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski [“ZBIG-nyev breh-ZIN-skee”] were on the American team that negotiated these agreements. American officials kept rewriting a single draft text and carrying it between the two other delegations.
tossups.r: These agreements are named for the Maryland retreat where the talks took place. For 10 points, name these 1978 accords negotiated by Jimmy Carter, Anwar Sadat, and Menachem Begin.

tossups.p: Israel’s Foreign Minister Moshe Dayan and Defense Minister Ezer Weizman took part in the talks that led to these agreements. One of these agreements set out a plan for a peace treaty in which Israel would give back land it had taken in 1967.
tossups.r: That land was the Sinai Peninsula. For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements between Egypt and Israel.

tossups.p: Lawrence Wright’s 2014 book _Thirteen Days in September_ tells the story of the talks that produced these agreements. During those talks, the host kept the leaders and their teams together, away from reporters, at a guarded retreat in the Catoctin Mountains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 Middle East peace agreements, named for a presidential retreat in Maryland.

tossups.p: The site of the talks that produced these agreements was called “Shangri-La” by Franklin Roosevelt, after a hidden paradise in James Hilton’s novel _Lost Horizon_. In 1953, Dwight Eisenhower renamed that presidential retreat in honor of his father and his grandson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements between Egypt and Israel, named for that Maryland retreat.

tossups.p: The talks that produced these agreements took place at a presidential retreat run by the U.S. Navy, which is officially named Naval Support Facility Thurmont, inside Maryland’s Catoctin Mountain Park. The leaders and their teams stayed in cabins there for thirteen days in September 1978.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements reached by Jimmy Carter, Anwar Sadat of Egypt, and Menachem Begin of Israel.

tossups.p: In November 1977, one leader who later signed these agreements flew to Jerusalem and spoke to the Knesset [“kuh-NESS-it”], becoming the first Arab head of state to visit Israel. Less than a year later, he met the Israeli prime minister in Maryland.
tossups.r: That leader was Anwar Sadat of Egypt. For 10 points, name these 1978 agreements brokered by Jimmy Carter.

tossups.p: One of these agreements called for Palestinian self-government in the West Bank and Gaza during a five-year transition period, but that plan was never carried out. The other set the terms for a peace treaty between two neighboring countries.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 accords between Egypt and Israel, signed after talks at a Maryland retreat.

tossups.p: After one country signed a treaty based on these agreements, the Arab League suspended it and moved the league’s headquarters out of that country’s capital to Tunis. That country was not readmitted until 1989.
tossups.r: That country was Egypt. For 10 points, name these 1978 accords brokered by Jimmy Carter between Egypt and Israel.

tossups.p: On October 6, 1981, one leader who signed these agreements was assassinated by extremists while watching a military parade in Cairo. His vice president, Hosni Mubarak, took over and kept the peace that these agreements had begun.
tossups.r: That leader was Anwar Sadat. For 10 points, name these 1978 accords that Sadat reached with Menachem Begin.

tossups.p: In 1982, an international force called the Multinational Force and Observers began patrolling a desert peninsula to support a treaty that grew out of these agreements. That year, Israel finished handing the peninsula back to Egypt.
tossups.r: That peninsula was the Sinai. For 10 points, name these 1978 accords brokered by Jimmy Carter.

tossups.p: Israel had captured a large desert peninsula from Egypt in the Six-Day War of 1967, and Egypt tried to win it back in the 1973 Yom Kippur War. These agreements led Israel to promise to return that land in exchange for peace and recognition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 accords, signed after Jimmy Carter hosted Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin in Maryland.

tossups.p: On March 26, 1979, leaders shook hands on the White House lawn after signing a peace treaty that grew out of these agreements. With that treaty, Egypt became the first Arab country to officially recognize Israel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 1978 accords negotiated at a Maryland retreat by Jimmy Carter, Anwar Sadat, and Menachem Begin.

tossups.p: Nikita Khrushchev [“KROOSH-chef”] met Dwight Eisenhower in 1959 at the retreat that names these agreements, and in 2000, Bill Clinton hosted talks there with Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat that ended without a deal. These agreements came out of an earlier summit there, in September 1978.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these accords between Egypt and Israel, brokered by Jimmy Carter for Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin.

trap.title: Accords, retreat, or treaty?
trap.body: This answer line has close neighbors. Camp David is the presidential retreat in Maryland, which also hosted Eisenhower and Khrushchev (1959) and a failed 2000 summit with Bill Clinton, Ehud Barak, and Yasser Arafat. The accords (1978) were frameworks for peace, and the actual Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty was signed in 1979. The Oslo Accords (1993) were a different agreement, between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization.
trap.fix: For “these agreements” or “these accords,” say “Camp David Accords” in full, since some answer lines only prompt on “Camp David.” If the question asks for “this treaty,” it may want the 1979 Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty; if it asks for “this retreat,” say Camp David.
