topics.name: Cape Cod
topics.kicker: Hook-shaped Massachusetts peninsula · The Pilgrims’ first landfall, 1620
topics.briefing: Cape Cod is a hook-shaped peninsula in Massachusetts that curls out into the Atlantic Ocean like a bent arm. In 1602, the English explorer Bartholomew Gosnold named it for the codfish his crew caught there, and in November 1620 the _Mayflower_ anchored at its tip, where the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact before settling at Plymouth. Later it became home to Marconi’s wireless station, the Kennedy family’s summer houses, and a national seashore.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the same 1602 voyage on which he named this place, an English explorer built a short-lived trading post on Cuttyhunk Island and named nearby Martha’s Vineyard. Five years later, he died at Jamestown, a colony he had helped organize.
tossups.r: That explorer, Bartholomew Gosnold, named this place for the fish his crew caught there. For 10 points, name this hook-shaped Massachusetts peninsula.

tossups.p: At a place later called Corn Hill, explorers took corn that Native people had stored in the ground. Weeks later, at a spot now called First Encounter Beach, those explorers had a brief clash with Nauset men in December 1620, but no one was killed.
tossups.r: Those explorers had arrived on the _Mayflower_. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula where the Pilgrims first landed in 1620.

tossups.p: Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of a granite tower on this peninsula in 1907, and the tower was finished in 1910. That tower, the Pilgrim Monument, rises above the town of Provincetown at this peninsula’s tip.
tossups.r: It honors the Pilgrims, whose _Mayflower_ first anchored here in 1620. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula.

tossups.p: Peregrine White, the first English child born in New England, was born aboard a ship anchored off this peninsula in November 1620. Days earlier, forty-one men had signed a famous agreement aboard that ship in the harbor at this peninsula’s tip.
tossups.r: That ship was the _Mayflower_. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula where the Pilgrims landed before settling at Plymouth.

tossups.p: On January 18, 1903, Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless station at South Wellfleet on this peninsula sent a greeting from Theodore Roosevelt to King Edward VII. The king’s reply made it one of the first two-way wireless exchanges across the Atlantic.
tossups.r: That site later became part of a national seashore created by John F. Kennedy. For 10 points, name this hook-shaped Massachusetts peninsula.

tossups.p: August Belmont Jr.’s company opened a canal across this peninsula’s base in 1914, and the federal government bought it in 1928. In 1935, the Bourne and Sagamore Bridges opened to carry cars over that canal.
tossups.r: That canal lets ships avoid sailing around its dangerous outer shore. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, where the _Mayflower_ first anchored in 1620.

tossups.p: In 1961, John F. Kennedy signed a law creating a national seashore that protects about forty miles of this peninsula’s beaches, dunes, and marshes. Kennedy’s family had long spent summers in a group of houses at Hyannis Port here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, which the explorer Bartholomew Gosnold named for a fish.

tossups.p: “A man may stand there and put all America behind him,” wrote Henry David Thoreau about the outer beach of this peninsula. Thoreau’s book about walking its shores was published in 1865, three years after his death.
tossups.r: That book shares its name with this place. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, where the Pilgrims first landed.

tossups.p: Henry Beston spent a year living in a small cottage on a beach in Eastham on this peninsula and described the seasons there in _The Outermost House_. A blizzard washed that cottage out to sea in 1978.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hook-shaped Massachusetts peninsula, home to a national seashore and the town of Provincetown.

tossups.p: In 1984, divers led by Barry Clifford found the wreck of the _Whydah_, a pirate ship that sank in a storm off this peninsula in 1717. The ship’s captain, “Black Sam” Bellamy, died in the wreck along with most of his crew.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, at whose tip lies the town of Provincetown, where the Pilgrims first landed.

tossups.p: In 2007, the Mashpee Wampanoag [“wahm-puh-NOH-ag”] Tribe of this peninsula was recognized as a tribe by the U.S. government. The Nauset, a related people, lived on the outer part of this peninsula when English settlers arrived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula where the _Mayflower_ anchored in 1620, before the Pilgrims settled at Plymouth.

tossups.p: This landform was built from sand and gravel left behind by melting glaciers at the end of the last ice age. Its shape is often compared to a bent arm, with its “elbow” at Chatham and its “fist” at Provincetown.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, where the Pilgrims first anchored in 1620 aboard the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: Around 1816, Captain Henry Hall of the town of Dennis is said to have started growing cranberries as a crop on this peninsula. Its oldest town, Sandwich, was incorporated in 1639, when the area belonged to Plymouth Colony.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hook-shaped peninsula in Massachusetts, named for a fish that early explorers caught there.

tossups.p: In 1916, the Provincetown Players staged Eugene O’Neill’s first play to be performed, _Bound East for Cardiff_, in a fishing-wharf theater on this peninsula. The painter Edward Hopper later spent decades of summers working at his studio in Truro here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, where the Kennedy family kept summer homes at Hyannis Port.

tossups.p: In 1952, four Coast Guardsmen in a small lifeboat from Chatham rescued 32 sailors from the tanker _Pendleton_, which had broken in two during a storm off this peninsula. That rescue is the subject of the 2016 film _The Finest Hours_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts peninsula, where the Pilgrims first landed in 1620 before moving on to Plymouth.

clues.t: Hook-shaped peninsula in southeastern Massachusetts, curling into the Atlantic like a bent arm
The _Mayflower_ anchored at its tip in November 1620, before the Pilgrims settled at Plymouth
Named in 1602 by English explorer Bartholomew Gosnold for the codfish his crew caught there
The Kennedy family kept summer homes at Hyannis Port, John F. Kennedy’s “Summer White House”
The Mayflower Compact was signed aboard ship in what is now Provincetown Harbor, at the very tip
A canal opened across its base in 1914, so ships no longer had to sail around its dangerous outer shore
John F. Kennedy signed the law creating its national seashore in 1961
Guglielmo Marconi’s station at South Wellfleet exchanged wireless messages with Britain in 1903
Built from moraines and other sand and gravel left by melting glaciers at the end of the last ice age
Homeland of Wampanoag peoples; the Nauset lived on the outer part, and the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe won federal recognition in 2007
Pilgrim explorers took stored corn at Corn Hill and clashed with Nauset men at First Encounter Beach (December 1620)
Henry David Thoreau wrote a book about walking its beaches (1865): “A man may stand there and put all America behind him”
On his 1602 voyage, Gosnold also named Martha’s Vineyard and built a short-lived post on Cuttyhunk Island; he later died at Jamestown
Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone (1907) of the Pilgrim Monument, a granite tower in Provincetown finished in 1910
Peregrine White, the first English child born in New England, was born aboard the _Mayflower_ while it lay at anchor here
Marconi’s station sent Theodore Roosevelt’s greeting to King Edward VII on January 18, 1903
August Belmont Jr.’s company built the canal; the government bought it in 1928, and the Bourne and Sagamore Bridges opened in 1935
Henry Beston’s _The Outermost House_ describes a year in his beach cottage in Eastham; a 1978 blizzard washed the cottage away
The pirate ship _Whydah_ of “Black Sam” Bellamy sank off its coast in 1717; Barry Clifford’s divers found it in 1984
Its oldest town, Sandwich, was incorporated in 1639, when the area belonged to Plymouth Colony
Captain Henry Hall of Dennis is said to have begun growing cranberries as a crop here around 1816
The Provincetown Players staged Eugene O’Neill’s _Bound East for Cardiff_ in a wharf theater in 1916
Painter Edward Hopper spent decades of summers working at his studio in Truro
In 1952, four Coast Guardsmen from Chatham rescued 32 sailors from the broken tanker _Pendleton_ (_The Finest Hours_, 2016)
Its fifteen towns make up Barnstable County

trap.title: Peninsula, not state
trap.body: Cape Cod questions are full of places that are answer lines of their own: Massachusetts (the state it belongs to), Plymouth Colony (where the Pilgrims settled after leaving the Cape), and the _Mayflower_ (their ship). Nearby islands such as Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket, and other capes like Cape Ann and Cape Canaveral, are also wrong.
trap.fix: If the question says “this peninsula” or “this cape,” answer Cape Cod, not Massachusetts or Plymouth. Where the _Mayflower_ first anchored, Provincetown, Hyannis Port, Wellfleet, and Bartholomew Gosnold’s codfish all point to Cape Cod. Saying only “the Cape” earns a prompt, so add “Cod.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Cape Cod (prompt on Cape; do not accept “Massachusetts”)

topics.name: Carrie Nation
topics.kicker: Hatchet-swinging temperance activist · Smashed Kansas saloons from 1900
topics.briefing: Carrie Nation stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had called her to destroy saloons. Kansas had already banned alcohol, but illegal bars stayed open, so starting in 1900 she marched into them and smashed bottles, mirrors, and furniture, first with rocks and then with her famous hatchet. She was arrested about 30 times, paid her fines partly by selling souvenir hatchets, and died in 1911, nine years before national Prohibition began.
topics.answerHtml: Carrie Nation (or Carry A. Nation; accept Carrie Amelia Moore Nation)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This woman was born in Garrard County, Kentucky, in 1846, and she died in Leavenworth, Kansas, in 1911. Her gravestone in Belton, Missouri, says “She hath done what she could” and calls her “Faithful to the Cause of Prohibition.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed Kansas saloons with a hatchet starting in 1900.

tossups.p: This woman’s first husband, Dr. Charles Gloyd, drank heavily and died about two years after their wedding; she blamed alcohol for ruining her marriage. Years later, she helped start a local chapter of a women’s temperance group in Medicine Lodge, Kansas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who later attacked saloons with a hatchet, starting in 1900.

tossups.p: In 1901, this woman’s second husband, a lawyer and minister named David, divorced her, saying she had deserted him. He was nineteen years older than she was. That same year, she began publishing a newspaper called _The Smasher’s Mail_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist famous for attacking saloons with a hatchet in Kansas.

tossups.p: In June 1900, this woman said a vision told her to go to Kiowa, Kansas, and smash its saloons. She rode there in a buggy loaded with rocks and bricks and threw them at the bottles and mirrors in the town’s illegal bars.
tossups.r: Later she began using a hatchet instead. For 10 points, name this Kansas temperance activist.

tossups.p: In December 1900, this woman smashed a large mirror and bottles at the bar of the Carey Hotel in Wichita, Kansas, and was arrested. Weeks later, she began carrying the tool that became her symbol.
tossups.r: That tool was a hatchet. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed saloons in Kansas.

tossups.p: In 1901, this woman took her campaign to Topeka, the capital of Kansas, smashing saloons there and demanding that officials enforce the state’s ban on alcohol. Kansas had banned alcohol in its constitution since 1881.
tossups.r: She belonged to the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this activist who attacked illegal bars with a hatchet.

tossups.p: This woman described herself as “a bulldog running along at the feet of Jesus, barking at what He doesn’t like.” She stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had chosen her to destroy saloons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Kansas activist who smashed bars with a hatchet, beginning in 1900.

tossups.p: This woman was arrested about thirty times, and she paid her fines with money from lectures and appearances on vaudeville stages. Crowds came to hear the nearly six-foot-tall speaker describe her raids on bars.
tossups.r: She also sold souvenir pins shaped like a hatchet, her symbol. For 10 points, name this temperance activist from Kansas.

tossups.p: After Kansas banned alcohol in 1881, illegal saloons there were known as “joints,” and their owners as “jointists.” This woman began wrecking joints in 1900, arguing that because the bars broke the law, they could be destroyed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist who used a hatchet in her attacks.

tossups.p: This woman favored a spelling of her first name that turned her full name, with her middle initial, into a slogan, and she registered that version as a trademark. Her autobiography describes her visions and her raids on bars.
tossups.r: That spelling was “Carry.” For 10 points, name this temperance activist known for smashing saloons with a hatchet.

tossups.p: This woman gave her last public speech in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, in January 1911, collapsing after declaring, “I have done what I could.” She died that June in a hospital in Leavenworth, Kansas.
tossups.r: Her home in Eureka Springs was called Hatchet Hall. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed saloons.

tossups.p: Douglas Moore, the composer of _The Ballad of Baby Doe_, wrote a 1966 opera about this woman that premiered at the University of Kansas. In real life, she lived for years in Medicine Lodge, Kansas, where her house is a National Historic Landmark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this activist who attacked saloons with a hatchet, a member of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union.

tossups.p: The temperance group this woman joined was founded in Cleveland in 1874 and was led for nearly twenty years by Frances Willard, whose “Do Everything” policy included women’s suffrage. This woman started a local chapter of that group in Kansas.
tossups.r: That group was the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this member who smashed Kansas saloons with a hatchet.

tossups.p: A famous photograph shows this woman in a long dark dress, holding a Bible in one hand. She believed saloons ruined families by leaving wives and children poor while men spent their wages on drink.
tossups.r: In her other hand, she holds a hatchet. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed Kansas saloons.

tossups.p: While the Anti-Saloon League lobbied lawmakers to ban alcohol, this woman took direct action, walking into illegal Kansas bars and destroying their stock and furniture. Nine years after her 1911 death, the 18th Amendment brought nationwide Prohibition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this activist who swung a hatchet in her raids on saloons.

clues.t: Smashed saloons with a hatchet; she called her attacks “hatchetations”
Began wrecking illegal saloons in Kansas in 1900
A member of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU), founded in 1874
Fought for prohibition (banning alcohol); she died in 1911, nine years before the 18th Amendment took effect
Said a vision sent her to Kiowa, Kansas, where she smashed saloons with rocks and bricks (June 1900)
Lived in Medicine Lodge, Kansas, where she helped start a local WCTU chapter; her house there is a National Historic Landmark
Kansas had banned alcohol in its constitution since 1881, so the bars (“joints”) she attacked were illegal
Called herself “a bulldog running along at the feet of Jesus, barking at what He doesn’t like”
Arrested about 30 times; paid her fines with lecture and vaudeville money and sales of souvenir hatchet pins
Her first husband, Dr. Charles Gloyd, drank heavily and died about two years after their wedding
In December 1900, she smashed the bar of the Carey Hotel in Wichita
Famous photos show her holding a Bible in one hand and a hatchet in the other
Stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had chosen her to destroy saloons
Published a newspaper called _The Smasher’s Mail_ (1901)
Favored the spelling “Carry,” which made her full name a slogan, and registered that version as a trademark
Her second husband, David, a lawyer and minister 19 years older, divorced her in 1901, saying she had deserted him
In 1901, she smashed saloons in Topeka, the Kansas capital, and demanded that officials enforce the ban
Gave her last speech in Eureka Springs, Arkansas (January 1911), collapsing after saying “I have done what I could”; her home there was Hatchet Hall
Buried in Belton, Missouri; her stone reads “Faithful to the Cause of Prohibition, She Hath Done What She Could”
Born in Garrard County, Kentucky (1846); died in a hospital in Leavenworth, Kansas (1911)
Subject of a 1966 opera by Douglas Moore (composer of _The Ballad of Baby Doe_), first staged at the University of Kansas
Unlike the Anti-Saloon League (founded 1893), which lobbied lawmakers, she took direct action against bars

trap.title: Smasher or suffragist?
trap.body: Temperance and women’s rights clues overlap. Carrie Nation smashed saloons; Frances Willard led the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union for nearly twenty years; and Carrie Chapman Catt, another “Carrie,” led the final push for the 19th Amendment. Real tossups about the ban itself want Prohibition or the 18th Amendment, not her.
trap.fix: A hatchet, Kansas saloons, Kiowa, Medicine Lodge, and “hatchetations” mean Carrie Nation. Women’s suffrage and the 19th Amendment point to Catt or Susan B. Anthony, and “this law” or “this era” of banning alcohol means Prohibition. Her last name alone, “Nation,” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Carrie Nation (or Carry A. Nation; accept Carrie Amelia Moore Nation)

topics.name: Central Intelligence Agency
topics.kicker: U.S. foreign intelligence agency · Created by the National Security Act, 1947
topics.briefing: The Central Intelligence Agency gathers secret information about other countries to help U.S. presidents make decisions, and it sometimes carries out covert operations overseas. It was created in 1947 by the National Security Act, which Harry Truman signed, and grew out of World War II’s Office of Strategic Services. Based in Langley, Virginia, it ran the U-2 spy plane program in the 1950s and planned the failed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in 1961.
topics.answerHtml: Central Intelligence Agency (accept CIA; prompt on Langley or the Company; do not accept “FBI” or “NSA”)
reject: office of the director of national intelligence

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Rear Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter [“HILL-en-ket-er”] served as the first director of this agency from 1947 to 1950. The same 1947 law that created this agency also created the National Security Council and made the Air Force a separate branch of the military.
tossups.r: That law was the National Security Act, signed by Harry Truman. For 10 points, name this spy agency headquartered in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: William “Wild Bill” Donovan, who had won the Medal of Honor in World War I, led the World War II spy service from which this agency grew. Harry Truman broke up that wartime service, the Office of Strategic Services, in 1945.
tossups.r: Two years later, Truman signed the law that created this agency. For 10 points, name this foreign intelligence agency based in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: Allen Dulles, whose brother John Foster Dulles was Secretary of State, became this agency’s longest-serving director, leading it from 1953 to 1961. John F. Kennedy forced Dulles out after a failed invasion this agency had planned.
tossups.r: That invasion landed at Cuba’s Bay of Pigs. For 10 points, name this American spy agency.

tossups.p: In 1953, Kermit Roosevelt Jr., a grandson of Theodore Roosevelt, led this agency’s operation to help overthrow Iran’s prime minister, Mohammad Mosaddegh [“moh-sah-DEK”]. The next year, this agency backed a coup that drove Guatemala’s president, Jacobo Árbenz [“AR-bens”], from power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this U.S. spy agency created in 1947 and based in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: Richard Bissell ran this agency’s program to build and fly a high-altitude spy plane, which began test flights in Nevada in 1955. In 1960, one of those planes was shot down over the Soviet Union, and its pilot, Francis Gary Powers, was captured.
tossups.r: That plane was the U-2. For 10 points, name this American spy agency, which also planned the Bay of Pigs invasion.

tossups.p: In 1962, Francis Gary Powers was traded for the Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin’s Glienicke [“GLEE-nih-kuh”] Bridge, a story told in the Steven Spielberg film _Bridge of Spies_. Powers had been flying a spy plane for this agency when he was shot down.
tossups.r: That spy plane was the U-2. For 10 points, name this American spy agency headquartered in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: This agency trained about 1,400 Cuban exiles of Brigade 2506 under a plan drawn up during Dwight Eisenhower’s presidency. In April 1961, those exiles landed at Playa Girón [“hee-ROHN”] and were defeated within days by Fidel Castro’s forces.
tossups.r: That landing was the Bay of Pigs invasion. For 10 points, name this U.S. spy agency.

tossups.p: In 1975, a Senate committee led by Frank Church of Idaho investigated this agency’s secret plots to kill foreign leaders such as Fidel Castro. The next year, Gerald Ford issued an executive order banning political assassinations by U.S. government employees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spy agency created by the National Security Act of 1947.

tossups.p: After Gerald Ford dismissed William Colby as this agency’s director in 1975, Ford chose a future president to lead it in 1976 and 1977. In 1999, this agency’s headquarters was named for that man.
tossups.r: That man was George H. W. Bush. For 10 points, name this spy agency based in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: Jim Sanborn’s sculpture _Kryptos_, which holds four coded messages, stands outside this agency’s headquarters, and its last message resisted solvers for decades. Inside, a Bible verse in the lobby reads, “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
tossups.r: Stars on its Memorial Wall honor officers who died in its service. For 10 points, name this spy agency whose headquarters is in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: A copy of Bela Pratt’s statue of a Revolutionary War spy, whose original stands at Yale, was placed at this agency’s headquarters. A statue of William Donovan, who led this agency’s World War II forerunner, stands in its lobby.
tossups.r: The Revolutionary War spy was Nathan Hale. For 10 points, name this American spy agency created in 1947.

tossups.p: James Jesus Angleton led this agency’s counterintelligence staff for twenty years, searching for Soviet moles inside it. Long after Angleton left, one of this agency’s officers, Aldrich Ames, was arrested in 1994 for spying for the Soviet Union and Russia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American spy agency based in Langley, Virginia, which ran the U-2 program.

tossups.p: In 1980, this agency’s officer Tony Mendez helped six American diplomats escape from Iran by disguising them as a Canadian film crew scouting locations for a fake science-fiction movie. Ben Affleck directed and starred in a 2012 film about that rescue.
tossups.r: That film was _Argo_. For 10 points, name this American spy agency headquartered in Langley, Virginia.

tossups.p: During the Vietnam War, this agency secretly owned an airline called Air America, which flew supplies for a secret war in Laos in which Hmong [“MONG”] fighters battled communist forces. This agency is often nicknamed “the Company.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American spy agency, which has no police powers inside the United States, unlike the FBI.

tossups.p: After the 9/11 attacks, a 2004 law created a Director of National Intelligence, ending this agency’s director’s role as head of the U.S. intelligence community. This agency’s officers later tracked Osama bin Laden to Abbottabad [“AB-uh-tuh-bahd”], Pakistan.
tossups.r: He was killed there in a 2011 raid by U.S. Navy SEALs. For 10 points, name this American spy agency based in Langley, Virginia.

trap.title: Which three letters?
trap.body: Several agencies get mixed up. The CIA gathers intelligence abroad and has no police powers at home; the FBI, part of the Justice Department, investigates federal crimes and catches spies inside the United States; and the NSA intercepts and decodes communications. The CIA’s World War II forerunner was the Office of Strategic Services (OSS), and the Soviet Union’s spy agency was the KGB.
trap.fix: Spying abroad, Langley, the OSS, Allen Dulles, the U-2, the Bay of Pigs, and the Church Committee mean the CIA. J. Edgar Hoover, G-men, and the Ten Most Wanted list mean the FBI. If the question asks for “this law,” the answer may be the National Security Act of 1947.
trap.line: Real answer line: Central Intelligence Agency (accept CIA; prompt on Langley or the Company; do not accept “FBI” or “NSA”)
